topic: The Magic of Dandelin Spheres: Linking Cones to Ellipses
target_audience: High school students (Advanced Geometry) and undergraduate math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Mystery of the Sliced Cone
sections.content: Introduce the concept of conic sections by visualizing a plane intersecting a solid cone. Establish the 'why'—we know the result is an ellipse, but how can we prove it follows the geometric definition (the sum of distances to two foci is constant)?
sections.example: A 'Geometry Chef' character uses a laser to slice through a conical carrot. As the slice is tilted, the cross-section changes from a circle to an elongated oval. The Chef asks: 'How do we find the secret heart (foci) of this carrot slice?'

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Two-Tangent Theorem
sections.content: Before the main proof, refresh the 'Ice Cream Cone' theorem: From any point outside a sphere, the lengths of the two tangent segments to the sphere are equal. This is the crucial logical building block for the Dandelin proof.
sections.example: An animation shows a point 'P' outside a basketball. Two strings are pulled tight from P to touch the ball at points A and B. A ruler appears to show that segment PA is always equal to segment PB, no matter how the ball rotates.

sections.title: Enter the Dandelin Spheres
sections.content: Introduce the 'Dandelin Spheres': two spheres placed inside the cone, one above the cutting plane and one below. Each sphere is perfectly sized to be tangent to both the cone (along a circle) and the cutting plane (at a single point).
sections.example: Visualize two glowing bubbles expanding inside a glass funnel until they get 'stuck' against a tilted glass sheet (the cutting plane). The points where the bubbles touch the sheet are labeled F1 and F2.

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: The Geometric Proof
sections.content: Pick an arbitrary point 'P' on the elliptical cross-section. Show that the distance from P to the focus (F1) is equal to the distance from P to the upper circle of tangency along the cone's surface. Repeat for the lower sphere (F2). The sum of these distances is the constant length along the cone between the two circles of tangency.
sections.example: Color-coded lines (Red for upper sphere, Blue for lower) trace from point P to the foci. The animation 'unfolds' these lines onto the surface of the cone, showing they form a straight segment of fixed length along the cone's slant, proving PF1 + PF2 = Constant.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Harmony
sections.content: Recap how Dandelin's elegant 1822 construction bridges the gap between 3D intersections and 2D focal definitions. Briefly mention that this works for parabolas and hyperbolas with slight adjustments to the sphere placement.
sections.example: A montage shows the 'Geometry Chef' using these focal points to perfectly position orbit paths for a satellite (elliptical orbit) around a planet, demonstrating that the beauty of Dandelin spheres governs the stars.
